BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: High pressure will build in on Thursday with a warm front bringing another push of precipitation and much higher snow levels for Thursday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Patchy fog will continue through the late morning in southeast Oregon valleys.
- Next round of precipitation with limited accumulations passes late tonight into early Monday.
- A generally unsettled and wet pattern will continue through next week, with brief dry periods today and next Tuesday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: High pressure will continue to build into the region today, bringing cool and dry conditions. Clearing aloft overnight has allowed for rapid radiational cooling, especially in southeast Oregon. Temperatures in Burns, OR have plummeted down to 11F. Areas of fog have formed in these higher elevation valleys in southeast Oregon, with mid level clouds and low stratus in southwest Idaho preventing rapid cooling.

A closed low near the PacNW Coast will eject a shortwave trough across the region late this evening through Sunday, with precipitation favoring higher terrain in southeast Oregon and in central Idaho. Snow showers will begin in eastern Oregon late Saturday, with a weak frontal passage moving through southwest Idaho on Sunday and Monday. Minimal accumulations are anticipated with this frontal passage, but colder air at higher elevations in the West Central/Boise Mountains will allow for accumulations between 1- 3 inches by Monday morning. Rain will be the predominant precipitation type in the Snake River Valley, with a low chance of a brief rain-snow mix on Monday morning. High pressure will build back in late Monday through Tuesday, bringing a return to dry conditions, with a slight warming trend.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: A complex upper level pattern will continue to bring several rounds of precipitation, breezy winds, and fluctuating temperatures through the long term period. Another closed low in the Eastern Pacific will shift east on Tuesday, pushing a pronounced atmospheric river into northern California, Oregon and southern Washington. Remnants of this substantial moisture will move into the region on Wednesday, with some model disagreement on how much moisture will make it into our region on Wednesday. The best chances of precipitation will be over southeast Oregon on Wednesday, with high terrain in southwestern Idaho also seeing elevated chances.

High pressure will build in on Thursday with a warm front bringing another push of precipitation and much higher snow levels for Thursday. Some deterministic solutions show snow levels reaching near 7000 feet MSL on Thursday, with current forecast favoring lower levels near 5500-6500 feet MSL. Dry and warm conditions will continue through Saturday, with another system threatening to move into the region on Sunday. Model uncertainty remains high for next weekend's system, with current forecast favoring only a 20-30% chance of measurable precipitation over the region.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: Another weakening upper level trough is set to move through the area Monday afternoon/evening, bringing another round of 1.0 to 2.0 inch snow totals for our mountains.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Another system brings the chance for mountain snow showers late Monday.
- Cooler fall temperatures to continue through mid next week.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: The positively tilted upper level trough over the Great Basin continues to slide east this morning, weakening as it tracks over Colorado Saturday afternoon. The southwest jet ahead of this wave which was responsible for the widespread gusty winds Friday afternoon also begins to weaken and become more southerly. As previous AFDs have stated, this system will bring another round of snow showers to our mountains, this time favoring the central mountains and southern Front Range. We have increased snow accumulations a tad to better reflect recent trends, with totals now ranging between 1.0 and 2.0 inches.

The chance for some snowflakes falling over the Denver metro still exists, and as the finer details become more clear, there are a few features that we have been examining. First, although the trough passing over the region looks quite weak, it will still bring some favorable ingredients for synoptic ascent. One of these ingredients would be the position of the right-entrance region of an embedded jet streak, favoring ascent over the Denver metro sometime Saturday morning. Other features that would promote and/or indicate QG ascent would be the passage of the remaining PV anomaly, and strong positive vorticity advection, albeit these will be at their strongest just to our south and east. At the same time, both global model solutions and CAMs suggest an area of frontogenesis at the 700mb level oriented SW-NE, extending from the central mountains and across Denver. This area of frontogenesis could be the key for the development of a more organized snowband. At the lowest levels, surface winds Saturday morning are expected to remain light (<8 mph). However, guidance has continued to suggest a broad anticyclonic circulation east of Denver, which could help promote some weak upsloping if positioned at just the right spot. The most obvious limiting factor appears to be moisture, with model soundings showing dry air near the surface that will need to be overcome for snowfall to reach the lower elevations. With all of these ingredients in mind, we have concluded that there is about a 30% chance for light snow accumulations (up to 0.5 in.) at the lower foothills and east over parts of the urban corridor. However, snowfall is likely to occur along a narrow band, meaning that only a small portion of our area will end up experiencing the first snowflakes of the season at low elevations. We expect this to be a very low-impact event, with a high-end scenario (10% chance) snowfall amount of just under one inch. Snow activity should exit the area by around noon, with decreasing cloud cover and temperatures rising into the upper 30s and low 40s for the afternoon.

Sunday morning is shaping up to be quite chilly, particularly for our mountains and high valleys, where morning lows will dip into the teens and single digits under the mostly clear skies. For the Denver metro and plains, morning lows should have no problem dropping into the 20s, with perhaps even some upper teens over the usual cold spots. We are monitoring the potential for some freezing fog over the northeast Colorado plains Sunday morning, although reduced visibilities are likely to be the main impact. Afternoon temperatures will be similar to Saturday, generally in the 40s, due to high clouds filling in from the west ahead of the next disturbance.

Another weakening upper level trough is set to move through the area Monday afternoon/evening, bringing another round of 1.0 to 2.0 inch snow totals for our mountains. We are fairly confident in temperatures staying at seasonal averages or slightly below average through at least Wednesday. However, long-range guidance has trended slightly drier and warmer late next week and into next weekend, with perhaps only a few shortwave passages that would bring sporadic snow chances for the mountains, or a few snowflakes at best for the Denver metro and plains.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: More organized ridging is expected to return to the area Wednesday, initiating another warming trend.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Scattered snow showers are expected to persist Saturday, mainly in the afternoon and early evening, in Carbon County and areas along and north of the US-20 Corridor.
- Chilly temperatures will continue through Tuesday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: The disorganized upper level low continues to meander across the region this morning. Today will be somewhat unsettled once again with this feature nearby. GOES water vapor imagery shows a split trough approaching the area. The primary upper level low is positioned well to our north in southern Canada, while a secondary shortwave trough is analyzed in eastern Utah. Modest convergence around the 700-mb level and a bit of overrunning south of the boundary are producing some radar returns around Cheyenne eastward into the southern Nebraska panhandle. Dewpoint depressions are fairly significant this morning, so this activity is struggling to reach the ground. However, we may see some flurries/light showers in these areas through the morning hours. PoPs were kept below 15% though, as it seems unlikely that this activity will manage to produce measurable precipitation.

Drier air in the middle atmosphere is present over much of the area from about Saratoga to Chadron, though a surface front slowly slipping southward is producing low clouds along and north of the US- 20 corridor. Improved moisture is present to the northwest of the narrow dry region aloft, supporting continued snow shower activity around northern Carbon county and western Converse county. Expect this to increase in coverage this morning, and then further increase into the afternoon. Starting around noon, a reinforcing surface cold front will sweep into Converse county from the north as the axis of the primary upper level low nears. Fairly rapid surface pressure rises on the order of 1-2 mb per hour along with modest synoptic forcing for ascent from the positive vorticity advection aloft should support increasing snow shower coverage. In addition, we will have fairly steep lapse rates (for this time of year) around 7 to 7.5 C/km and a few hundred J/kg SBCAPE ahead of the front. As a result, expect convective snow showers to develop this afternoon and persist into the evening, primarily along the US-20 corridor and northward. A few may reach as far south as the North Platte River valley, but confidence is reduced south of the crest of the Pine Ridge, as north-northwest flow will aid ascent only north of the ridge. Similar forcing will be present in Carbon county this afternoon, but without the mechanical forcing from rising surface pressure. Still, expect snow showers to pick up mainly around the higher terrain but possibly spreading into the lower elevations of the county as well. Most of this activity will be quick hitting, so the areas mentioned above can generally expect a dusting to an inch or two, but snow coverage will not be continuous, so accumulations will be hit-or-miss as well. Still, these will have the potential to be locally intense, leading to fluctuating visibility and rapidly changing conditions for travelers. Snow squall parameters are around 1 to 2 in the area this afternoon, suggesting that we may need to watch for squall activity. PoPs were raised to the 30 to 50% range to account for this possibility. Elsewhere, breezy westerlies will continue today but high winds are not expected.

Once the upper level trough axis passes through the area this evening, we should see snow shower activity shut off quickly. Sunday morning will be fairly chilly as the surface high pressure system settles in over the area. There will be possibility for some shallow low clouds/fog over the Plains as the high pushes closer to the Laramie range, but the pressure difference is rather subtle and thus not a very clear signal for upslope ascent. Sunday's temperatures will be chilly across the area, with most in the upper 30s to lower 40s.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Transient ridging will try to build in over the area Sunday into Monday, but we won't see much of a warm-up if any. 700-mb temperatures peak in the morning and then drop down again through the day Monday as the next messy Pacific trough approaches the area. In addition, the surface high pressure system will remain entrenched over the plains while increasing cloud cover prevents much warming. The approaching system will be another disorganized, split trough without much moisture or organized lift. Most ensemble members have some light snow developing in the mountains Monday PM and continuing into Tuesday AM, but even orographic ascent looks fairly weak, tempering QPF expectations. The mountains may manage to pick up a few inches on the high end. Tuesday looks like another chilly day, but with more sunshine as the trough pushes off to the east. Westerly winds will also return, but high wind probabilities are only around 10%. These creep up slightly Tuesday night to around 30 to 40% as pressure/height gradients tighten.

More organized ridging is expected to return to the area Wednesday, initiating another warming trend. Highs should be near to a few degrees above seasonal averages, generally mid 40s to lower 50s, and then remain near that mark for the rest of the work-week (possibly adding a few degrees Thursday or Friday). There is quite a bit of model spread in the late week period around Thanksgiving Day. The overall evolution of the synoptic pattern will likely feature another disorganized, moisture-starved trough meandering through on Thursday, followed by riding re-establishing itself Friday. Ensembles have fairly good agreement within a given system, but are extremely divergent between suites (e.g. GEFS vs ECMWF ensemble). Nearly all GEFS members push the Thursday low so far to the south that our area remains entirely dry. Then, the resultant ridge Friday amplifies further north, centered over the Pacific Northwest, forcing the storm track and jet stream well to our north into Canada. This would lead to little to no precipitation anywhere in the area, significantly warmer temperatures, and lighter winds. Meanwhile, most ECMWF ensemble members are clustered around a solution that keeps the first upper level low closer to our area, bringing a chance for some light snow showers Wednesday night. Then, the developing ridge is strongest over the southwest CONUS instead of northwest, allowing the core of the Pacific jet to stream inland much closer to our area. This scenario would keep temperatures closer to seasonal averages, increase the potential for mountain snowfall Thursday and Friday, and also dramatically increase the potential for high winds across southeast Wyoming. The GEFS has generally been (anecdotally) performing better than the ECMWF ensemble at this lead time in recent weeks, but that doesn't necessarily mean it will continue to perform better. The official forecast represents a blend of these two somewhat equally likely scenarios.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: There continues to be a vague signal of another system passing through late next week, but models are not in good agreement. Some solutions depict wet weather, while others not so much.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Generally dry and cooler conditions for the majority of the weekend.
- Most desert valleys will likely see their first taste of below freezing overnight lows this weekend.
- Active weather remains possible for Thanksgiving week, but some details still remain uncertain. Stay tuned for updates to timing and impacts as they become available.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Light snow will continue to make its way out of the forecast area by this afternoon as the trough axis swings through. Local cameras in the San Juans appear to show a few inches of snow fell overnight, with snow still falling in some locations. Generally, as the cloud cover begins to burn off this morning, most locations will see sunny skies and decreased precipitation chances. Otherwise, temperatures have notably dropped behind the frontal boundary which passed through yesterday. This means that overnight lows for the next several nights are tracking to drop below freezing for a large swath of the area. Any valley locations which have yet to hit freezing will likely be hitting it sometime this weekend.

A low-amplitude ridge builds in behind the exiting trough Saturday evening into Sunday morning. This means that Sunday's weather will be relatively similar to Saturday. One point of note would be there is a possibility for clearing skies overnight into Sunday morning which could support localized fog in some valleys. The current forecast isn't overly bullish about this factor though, so there remains uncertainty. By Sunday evening, upper-level flow turns back to southwesterly ahead of an approaching trough. Moisture and forcing appear unimpressive with this system, so current expectations are for only light showers Sunday evening through Tuesday morning. Snow accumulations are on track to sit below advisory level.

There continues to be a vague signal of another system passing through late next week, but models are not in good agreement. Some solutions depict wet weather, while others not so much. Therefore, this far out, that forecast should be taken with a grain of salt. This potential storm could impact Thanksgiving travel, so stay tuned for additional updates to the forecast as those dates approach, especially if you plan on traveling for the holiday.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Dry weather with a gradual warming trend will return for the mid week time frame, then models diverge with the timing, amplitude and track of the next system over the Thanksgiving holiday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Upper trough will bring a round of snow across southern CO through Today with some light accumulations across the mountains.
- Below normal temperatures through next week with another system bringing light mountain snows and passing showers to the plains Monday into Monday night.
- Another system possible late week with mountain snows possible though model/ensemble consensus is trending drier for the southeast plains.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Upper trough out west will move across southern CO/northern NM today spreading snow from the Continental Divide into the southeast mountains and adjacent plains through the day. Strongest forcing will be this morning with 1 to 3 inches of additional snowfall for the mountain areas with the heaviest amounts along the Continental Divide. Orographic enhancement will initially favor the southwest mountains before shifting to the central mountains in the afternoon as flow becomes northwesterly behind the trough. But the atmosphere dries out quickly behind the trough axis too, so snow will diminish rapidly in the afternoon out west as the focus shifts eastward into the southeast mountains and adjacent plains. Overall, additional snow accumulations will remain light. A quick 1 to 2 inches of snow will be possible for portions of the southeast mountains with a quick round of forcing and steep lapse rates in the afternoon, but overall, amounts will be spotty and light. Portions of the Palmer Divide and Raton Mesa could see some snow showers in the afternoon, but little to no travel impacts are expected due to the residual ground warmth and brevity of the system.

Clearing skies tonight will lead to a cold night across southern Colorado. Low temperatures will drop into the single digits for some of the typical colder valley locations, with teens and 20s elsewhere.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Dry weather will return for Sunday with temperatures remaining below normal for most of the region. The next upper trough moves into the western U.S. Sunday night and will spread snow back into the Continental Divide on Monday and Monday night as it moves across Colorado as another open wave. Isolated to scattered showers may spill eastward onto the plains Monday night, but overall, any snow or precipitation amounts will remain light given the progressive nature of the system. Another 1 to 3 inches of snow will be possible along the Continental Divide, with a spotty inch or two across the remainder of the mountains. The plains could see a light dusting of snow overnight, though this will be localized and most areas may stay dry.

Dry weather with a gradual warming trend will return for the mid week time frame, then models diverge with the timing, amplitude and track of the next system over the Thanksgiving holiday. Canadian and EC and their ensembles bring another open trough across CO in the Wed/Thu timeframe, while GFS takes the majority of the energy/moisture much farther south into Old Mexico. GFS Ensemble means were more in line with the Canadian and EC. Given uncertainties, unsettled weather will continue with another round of mountain snows possible along the Continental Divide sometime late week. Forecast for the southeast plains leans dry for now with temperatures around seasonal averages.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: Conditions will get quiet again for Tuesday/Wednesday as a transient ridge develops. Guidance for the second half of next week is a bit more uncertain.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Snow showers linger across northern Utah overnight before drying out tomorrow.
- Freezing conditions expected tonight and tomorrow night for Zion and lower Washington county.
- Another weak storm is possible for Monday with snow as low as valley floors.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: The axis of the trough that has been bringing precipitation to northern Utah is currently just to the west of KSLC. This is bringing the coldest 700 mb temperatures (between -9 and -10C) over northern Utah with westerly flow aloft. This has kept showery activity on-and-off through much of the evening. This activity will continue, especially southeast and east of the Great Salt Lake which will provide some lake induced instability to initiate more showers overnight. These showers will be relatively brief, but as temperatures have cooled to near freezing across many locations a quick dusting of snow or graupel is possible across area roadways. Some of the hi-res guidance does want to develop a more organize band around sunrise tomorrow morning somewhere between Salt Lake City and Davis county. If this does develop then an inch or two of additional snow can't be ruled out.

High pressure redevelops over the area tomorrow which will help to bring drier conditions to the region, however temperatures will remain cooler than normal by about 5 degrees. This ridge will be short-lived as another lower amplitude trough moves into the Great Basin on Monday. 53% of ensemble members keep conditions relatively dry with this trough, while the other 47% of members bring light to moderate precipitation. With 700mb temperatures of -9C with this upcoming trough there should be enough cold air to support snow down to valley floors. Given that over 50% of members keep conditions relatively dry there is very little QPF in the 50th percentile (a few hundredths across the northern terrain), however there are some wetter members. The 90th percentile has 0.25-0.5" of QPF across northern Utah with a favored area across Weber and Davis counties as a result of the westerly flow expected with the incoming trough.

Conditions will get quiet again for Tuesday/Wednesday as a transient ridge develops. Guidance for the second half of next week is a bit more uncertain. ~50% of the members remain dry while the other 50% bring in moisture from an atmospheric river making landfall in the PNW. This moisture is ushered into northern Utah alongside northwesterly flow. This could bring appreciable moisture to the mountains of northern Utah if this pans out, so it will have to be something to watch to see which solution guidance trends towards.

2660.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Chris Dickson
bottom_line: Recent remote-triggered avalanches mean you should give a wide buffer to wind-drifted slopes near and above treeline to avoid triggering an avalanche that could bury you.

Very strong winds formed thicker and stiffer slabs on leeward slopes below ridgelines and in rocky gullies in the alpine. The most dangerous slopes face the north-half of the compass where weak snow lurks under these slabs. For safer travel options, seek out wind-sheltered areas. Conditions are safer below treeline.

2745.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Jason Konigsberg
bottom_line: There isn't enough snow for avalanches on most slopes. Steer around hard drifts of snow on steep terrain features and below ridgetop in the alpine.

3046.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

3014.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
bottom_line: Winter has begun to embrace the West Central Mountains of Idaho. 6-12 inches of new snow has fallen between Friday the 13th and Monday the 16th. Another 6-12 inches could stack up by the end of the week. If you're traveling in the mountains this week, watch out for wind slabs 1-2 feet thick above 7,000 feet and pay attention to terrain traps.
We'll update the General Avalanche Information weekly until full-time forecasting operations begin.
hazard_discussion: From 60-degree temperatures to over a foot of new snow, the weather sure has changed quickly over the past week. A cooler and wetter weather pattern has taken shape over our region since Friday the 13th. As of Monday (16th) afternoon, some mountain locations have picked up 6-12 inches of new snow along with southerly winds gusting 20-30 MPH.
Wind Slabs
• Wind slabs could become reactive this week with over a foot of new snow and gusty winds. Wind slabs will be most sensitive just below ridgelines.
• Look for clues of wind-affected snow, such as drifts, dunes, pillows, and freshly built cornices.
• Watch for signs of instability, such as shooting cracks. If you're observing these signs, find another aspect away from wind-drifted snow.
• Strong winds and local terrain features can alter the prevailing wind direction. Pay attention to cross-loading and wind-loading on unsuspecting slopes.
Early Season Conditions
• If you're out hiking or hunting in the mountains this fall, stay tuned to changing weather conditions. Avalanches are most likely during and immediately after a storm.

• Keep in mind the adage, "If there's enough snow to ride, there's enough snow to slide". Even if there's not enough snow to bury you, a small slide over uncovered logs, rocks, and brush would not be a fun way to start the season.
• Stay up to date on mountain weather with our WEATHER tab, where you'll find webcams, weather stations, and weather forecasting tools.
Check Your Winter Gear

• Beacons, shovels, probes, airbags. Run through all your gear and make sure it's functioning properly. Does your transceiver or airbag need any firmware updates? Look for cracks, defects, or corroded batteries. Make it fun with your friends and do a pre-season gear check with your winter travel companions.
Continuing Education
• Check out the Education tab on our website to sign up for avalanche courses this winter (COURSES ).
• Stay tuned to our EVENTS pages for other local happenings with the winter community.
• Interested in attending a snow and avalanche workshop (SAW)? Check out A3's WEBSITE for a list of events.
Observations
• Keep an eye on our observation page HERE

• If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation HERE. Early season observations help forecasters and the public alike. A simple photo and/or weather observation helps paint the picture of where snow is and where it is not.

Yeah, that's right: the Payette Avalanche Center has a new website. Browse around before the snow starts flying. We're also on the Avy App. You can search for "Avy: Avalanche & Weather Info" in your app store on your mobile device.

2755.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Chris Dickson
bottom_line: Most slopes are generally safe from avalanches. You might be able to trigger a small avalanche where you encounter stiff, wind-drifted snow below ridgelines, on lee slopes, and around rocky outcrops in the alpine.
